title: Midland Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Midland wells have a 380 ft median depth, 6.9 gpm median yield, and estimated finished costs of $30,700-$50,000.
h1: Midland, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost Guide
intro_html: Buying land near Midland means dealing with mountain bedrock, not a predictable shallow groundwater setting. Records within 5 miles show a median well depth of 380 feet, a median reported yield of 6.9 gallons per minute, and a median static water level of 115 feet below the surface. Most permits are for domestic or household use, and nearly all named aquifers are fractured-bedrock systems. These records are useful for budgeting and due diligence, but a nearby well does not guarantee the same result on your lot.

sections.heading: Midland wells commonly reach fractured mountain rock
sections.html:
Midland’s permitted wells are predominantly in unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers, with 601 wells recorded that way. Another 12 wells name Fractured Granite and 3 name Fractured Crystalline. That geology makes depth depend heavily on where fractures occur beneath a particular parcel.

The median completed depth is 380 feet. The middle half runs from 225 to 500 feet, so a driller’s bid based on a standard shallow hole would be risky here. Nearly half of the wells fall between 300 and 600 feet, while the deepest record reaches 1,000 feet. Only 9% are under 100 feet.

sections.heading: What Midland wells produce for household use
sections.html:
Among the 246 wells with reported pump yields, the median is 6.9 gallons per minute. The middle half is 2.0 to 9.6 gallons per minute, which gives a reasonable planning range but not a promise for an untested parcel.

Yield records show 11% under 1 gallon per minute, 30% from 1 to 5, and 54% from 5 to 15. Only 6% report more than 15 gallons per minute. For a buyer, that low-yield group matters: storage tanks and careful water-use planning may be necessary. Confirm the well’s permitted use, production test, pump setting, and recovery before assuming it can support a larger home or additional fixtures.

sections.heading: The Midland water level looks broadly steady
sections.html:
Only 40 wells report static water levels, so this is a limited sample rather than a complete groundwater trend. Within that sample, the median depth to water is 115 feet, with the middle half from 66 to 171 feet below the surface.

The decade comparison shows a median of 115 feet in the 2010s and 118 feet in the 2020s. That small change does not, by itself, establish a declining water table. It does mean pump design and electrical planning should account for water being well below the ground surface. Ask for the original well construction report and recent static and pumping levels, rather than relying only on the regional median.

sections.heading: Permit history shows long-term drilling around Midland
sections.html:
Colorado DWR records contain 623 permitted wells within the study area, with 361 recorded as constructed. Construction and yield information is incomplete: 373 report total depth and 246 report pump yield. The newest permit year is 2025, so this is an active, continuing well area rather than a place represented only by older records.

Permit activity was highest in the 1990s with 158 permits and remained substantial in the 2000s with 144. The most active names in the records are Mountain Well Improvement LLC (Wiley, David D.), Woods Drilling Inc. (Woods, William D.), and Woods Drilling Inc. (Woods, William L.). Their records can help identify local drilling patterns, but a new bid still depends on access, geology, casing, grout, and the planned well location.

sections.heading: Budgeting a new well in Midland’s bedrock
sections.html:
The cost model for Midland’s fractured granite and gneiss uses a drilling rate of $65 to $100 per foot. At the area’s 380-foot median depth, the drilled hole alone works out to about $24,700 to $38,000. That is not the complete project price.

A finished well including the pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $30,700 to $50,000 at the median depth. A deeper hole, difficult access, extra casing or grout, and challenging trenching can move the actual bid higher. When comparing bids, verify what is included and ask how the contractor charges if the first target does not produce water. The depth distribution from 225 to 500 feet makes a written depth assumption especially important.

sections.heading: Checks before buying or building on a Midland lot
sections.html:
Water quality and site conditions deserve the same attention as yield. Mapping within about 10 miles shows 10 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 324 historic mine features, and 12 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those mapped features do not prove a problem on a specific parcel, but they justify a professional water test and a review of nearby land uses, mine workings, and drainage.

Most permits are for domestic or household use, representing 91% of the use mix. Stock use is listed on 12%, while irrigation is listed at 0%. Confirm the permit before planning gardens, livestock, or other uses. Also check septic setbacks, replacement-area requirements, driveway access for a drill rig, building envelopes, and the possibility of a dry or very low-yield hole. A DWR permit review and neighboring well records should be part of the purchase contract process.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Midland, Colorado?
faq.a: The median permitted well depth near Midland is 380 feet. The middle half runs from 225 to 500 feet, and the deepest record reaches 1,000 feet. Nearly half of recorded wells are between 300 and 600 feet. Because the area is fractured mountain bedrock, the depth on one parcel may differ substantially from a nearby well.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Midland, Colorado?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $65 to $100 per foot. At the 380-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $24,700 to $38,000. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $30,700 to $50,000. Access, casing, grout, depth, and difficult ground can change the final bid.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce near Midland?
faq.a: The median reported pump yield is 6.9 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 2.0 to 9.6 gallons per minute. Records show 11% under 1 gallon per minute and 54% between 5 and 15. Only 246 wells report yield, so buyers should obtain the specific well’s production test and recovery information.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Midland?
faq.a: The well records do not establish drinking-water safety. Nearby mapping includes 10 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 324 historic mine features, and 12 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the well for common drinking-water constituents and contaminants relevant to the parcel’s mine and land-use history. Review the results with a qualified water professional before relying on the supply.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping near Midland?
faq.a: The available static-level sample is limited to 40 wells. Its median depth to water was 115 feet in the 2010s and 118 feet in the 2020s. That small difference does not establish a declining water table. For a particular property, compare the construction report with recent static and pumping levels and confirm the pump is suitable for the measured depth.
